units.title: Aims, selection, and weight-bearing status
units.summary: Mobility and Walking Aids HHS4867 Functional Movement Science HHS4867J • Increase area of Base of support (BOS) • Better BALANCE – maintain the centre of gravity (CG) over BOS • Redistribute weight bearing area with decreased loading on injured part • Improve proprioception • Decrease pain • Assist weak muscles → Improve stability and independency Different Types of Walking Aids Walking > Axillary > Elbow > Quadripod > Stick Frame crutches crutches (large > small) Selection of Walking Aids Physiotherapist considers patient’s • Disability level • Stability • Muscles strength of both upper & lower limb • Coordination of upper & lower limb • Weight bearing status • Non-weight bearing (NWB) • Touch down (TDW) • Partial weight bearing (PWB) • Weight bear as tolerated (WBAT) • Full weight bearing (FWB) • Patient’s ability to manipulate the walking aids (both cognitive & physical status) Selection of Walking Aids Example: Facture right tibia with partial weight bearing (PWB) status • Younger adults using elbow crutches • Elderly using frame due to physical limitations, poorer stability & coordination/agility As patient’s ability improves or change in weight bearing status, progress to less stability & support ones

units.title: Types of walking aids
units.summary: Walking Elbow crutches Stick Quadripod Frame NWB / PWB/ Touch down FWB/WB as tolerated Stairs Suitable for: Elderly / Young adults / people Stroke Stroke/ people with sufficient muscle / people require less people without strength, UL and trunk support require sufficient stability and minimal stability coordination support Walking Frame Rollator • Maximum stability and widest base of support • Rollator (two/four wheels)- allow patient to gently push for moving forward. • Frame: lift up & placed forward BEFORE step out • Foldable design for easier transportation & storage • Sequence: Frame → bad leg → good leg Limitations of Walking Frame/Rollator ➢ Relatively difficult to store and transport ➢ NOT RECOMMENDED for stairs walking ➢ Slower gait speed (Rollator FASTER than frame) Axillary Crutches • Patients who require LESS support with better stability or support compared with walking frame/ rollator • allow more flexible gait patterns with faster pace • Fitting x 2: height of the crutches AND level of hand piece • Sequence depends on gait pattern
summary_sentences: Walking Elbow crutches Stick Quadripod Frame NWB / PWB/ Touch down FWB/WB as tolerated Stairs Suitable for: Elderly / Young adults / people Stroke Stroke/ people with sufficient muscle / people require less people without strength, UL and trunk support require sufficient stability and minimal stability coordination support
Walking Frame Rollator • Maximum stability and widest base of support • Rollator (two/four wheels)- allow patient to gently push for moving forward.
• Frame: lift up & placed forward BEFORE step out • Foldable design for easier transportation & storage • Sequence: Frame → bad leg → good leg
Limitations of Walking Frame/Rollator ➢ Relatively difficult to store and transport ➢ NOT RECOMMENDED for stairs walking ➢ Slower gait speed (Rollator FASTER than frame)

Axillary Crutches • Patients who require LESS support with better stability or support compared with walking frame/ rollator • allow more flexible gait patterns with faster pace • Fitting x 2: height of the crutches AND level of hand piece • Sequence depends on gait pattern

units.title: Gait patterns
units.summary: Gait patterns Gait pattern depends upon the patient’s status like balance weight-bearing status 1. Three-point gait pattern (3pt gait) ➢ Bilateral crutches or walker ➢ Used in NWB only ➢ Good side: FWB; Affected NWB ➢ At least 50% of body weight is transmitted through the upper limb. • UL strength, core stability & good lower limb must be assessed BEFORE attempting this gait pattern ➢ The energy cost is about TWICE as normal walking (more tiring) Modified 3pt gait pattern ➢ Requires two crutches or a walker Touch down weight bearing (TDWB) ➢ Good side FWB + Affected side Touch Down Partial weight bearing (PWB) ➢ Good side FWB + Affected side > 50% BW Sequence: Crutches → good leg 3pt gait Modified 3pt gait Gait Pattern Bilateral aid Bilateral aid → Good F → Bad F → Good F Bilateral Walking Aids (Frame or Crutches) Weight bearing status
summary_sentences: Gait patterns Gait pattern depends upon the patient’s status like balance weight-bearing status 1.
Three-point gait pattern (3pt gait) ➢ Bilateral crutches or walker ➢ Used in NWB only ➢ Good side: FWB; Affected NWB ➢ At least 50% of body weight is transmitted through the upper limb.
• UL strength, core stability & good lower limb must be assessed BEFORE attempting this gait pattern ➢ The energy cost is about TWICE as normal walking (more tiring)

Modified 3pt gait pattern ➢ Requires two crutches or a walker Touch down weight bearing (TDWB) ➢ Good side FWB + Affected side Touch Down Partial weight bearing (PWB) ➢ Good side FWB + Affected side > 50% BW Sequence: Crutches → good leg
3pt gait Modified 3pt gait Gait Pattern Bilateral aid Bilateral aid → Good F → Bad F → Good F Bilateral Walking Aids (Frame or Crutches) Weight bearing status

units.title: Stairs
units.summary: Stairs "GOOD goes UP to heaven, BAD goes DOWN to hell“ ➢ Carer ➢ Assist Bad side ➢ Upstairs: one step behind ➢ Downstairs: wide base, facing and one step in front of Client Stairs with One side aids (Stick or quad) ➢ Up stairs ➢ good leg ➢ carer one step BEHIND, assisting bad side ➢ Down stairs ➢ Aid ➢ Carer one step in front, facing client and assisting bad side Stairs with Crutches ➢ Non-weight bearing ➢ With rails ➢ Good side hand on rail, crutches on other hand ➢ Upstairs: Good leg → Crutches + bad leg ➢ Down stairs: Crutches + bad leg → good leg ➢ No rails ➢ Up-stairs: Good leg → Crutches + bad leg ➢ Down stairs: Crutches + bad leg → good leg
summary_sentences: Stairs "GOOD goes UP to heaven, BAD goes DOWN to hell“ ➢ Carer ➢ Assist Bad side ➢ Upstairs: one step behind ➢ Downstairs: wide base, facing and one step in front of Client
Stairs with One side aids (Stick or quad) ➢ Up stairs ➢ good leg ➢ carer one step BEHIND, assisting bad side ➢ Down stairs ➢ Aid ➢ Carer one step in front, facing client and assisting bad side

Stairs with Crutches ➢ Non-weight bearing ➢ With rails ➢ Good side hand on rail, crutches on other hand ➢ Upstairs: Good leg → Crutches + bad leg ➢ Down stairs: Crutches + bad leg → good leg ➢ No rails ➢ Up-stairs: Good leg → Crutches + bad leg ➢ Down stairs: Crutches + bad leg → good leg
